name: Palm Sunday
description: Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. The start of Holy Week.
biblicalBasis: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey while the crowd lays cloaks and palm branches on the road, shouting 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!' (Matt 21:1-11, Mark 11:1-11, Luke 19:28-44, John 12:12-19). Jesus weeps over Jerusalem: 'If you had only known on this day what would bring you peace.' The fulfillment of Zechariah 9:9 concerning the humble king.
significance: Jesus comes as a king, but on a donkey—the Prince of Peace, not a warrior hero. The joy soon turns to 'Crucify him!' Palm Sunday reveals both Jesus' kingship and the fickleness of the crowd. He is hailed today and despised tomorrow. It is a day with two sides—joy and sorrow, praise and warning.
liturgicalContext: Violet or red color. A palm procession in many traditions. The Passion narrative (the full account of his suffering) is read in many churches on this Sunday. The start of Holy Week (Passion Week)—the week leading to the cross.
history: Palm Sunday was known in Jerusalem as early as the 4th century, when pilgrims carried palm branches in a procession from the Mount of Olives into the city. Egeria (c. 384) describes this procession. The custom spread to the Western Church throughout the Middle Ages.
otConnections: Zechariah 9:9: 'See, your king comes to you, righteous and having salvation, gentle and riding on a donkey.' Psalm 118:25-26: 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!'—the liturgical psalm from the Feast of Tabernacles. 1 Kings 1:32-40 concerning Solomon's anointing, where he rides on the king's mule.

references.reason: The main text for Palm Sunday: Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, the crowd's cry of 'Hosanna,' and the fulfillment of the prophecy about the humble king (verses 4-5).

This part of Matthew's account includes Jesus cleansing the temple (12-17), the parable of the fig tree (18-22), and the question regarding his authority (23-27). These events form a direct continuation of the Palm Sunday events in Jerusalem and are often read together in the liturgy.

The Parable of the Wedding Feast is part of the controversial teaching given by Jesus in Jerusalem during Holy Week before Easter. It explains why the invited guests (Israel's leaders) were rejected, which is contextually relevant to Palm Sunday's theme of the rejection of the invited King.

The question about paying taxes and the debate with the Sadducees are part of a series of confrontations between Jesus and the religious leaders in Jerusalem during Holy Week before Easter. These texts show Jesus' authority and the leaders' rejection of him, leading up to his crucifixion.

The confrontations with the Pharisees regarding the greatest commandment and the identity of the Messiah conclude the series of debates in the temple during Holy Week. The question about whether the Messiah is David's Lord (vv. 41-46) is directly relevant to Palm Sunday, where Jesus is hailed as David's son but also as the greater Lord.

Matthew 23 is a central part of the public teaching Jesus gives in Jerusalem during the week he is crucified. The text is directly linked to Palm Sunday through verse 39, where Jesus concludes with the prophecy that the people will not see him again until they say: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!' This is a direct quote from Psalm 118:26, which is the core of the Palm Sunday cry of 'Hosanna.' The chapter serves as a judgment against the religious leaders in Jerusalem just before the city's destruction and Jesus' entry.
